Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

Let $m,n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^{m+n}$ be open, and let
$F:U\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^1$.  Suppose $(a,b)\in U$, $F(a,b)=0$, and the
**partial derivative in the second block**

$$D_yF(a,b):\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n,\qquad D_yF(a,b)v:=DF(a,b)(0,v),$$

is invertible.  Put similarly $D_xF(a,b)u:=DF(a,b)(u,0)$.  Then there are open
neighbourhoods $P$ of $a$ and $Q$ of $b$, and a unique $C^1$ map
$\varphi:P\to Q$, such that

$$F(x,y)=0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad y=\varphi(x)\qquad((x,y)\in P\times Q).$$

After shrinking $P,Q$ if necessary, $D_yF(x,\varphi(x))$ is invertible and

$$D\varphi(x)=-D_yF(x,\varphi(x))^{-1}D_xF(x,\varphi(x)).$$

derivations.claim: Set $d_0(z)=1+|z|-z^2$ and $q_0=(z+x^2-y^2)/d_0(z)$ on $C$. Here $d_0\ge1$. For $z\ge0$, the largest numerator at fixed $z$ is $z+1-z^2=d_0$, with equality precisely at the points of $A_+$ at that height; the smallest numerator is $z-1+z^2\ge-d_0$, with equality only when $z=0$ and $x=0,y^2=1$. The corresponding inequalities for $z\le0$ follow by interchanging $x,y$ and replacing $z$ by $-z$. Thus $|q_0|\le1$ and equality occurs precisely on $A_+\cup A_-$. If $K$ is nonempty, let $m=\max_K|q_0|<1$ by [F1]; if $K$ is empty, put $m=0$. Choose $a=(1+m)/2$ and $b=(1+a)/2$.

Write $g(z)=\sqrt{z^2+\varepsilon^2}-\varepsilon$. Since $0\le |z|-g(z)\le\varepsilon$, we have $d=d_0-(|z|-g)\ge1-\varepsilon$ on $[-1,1]$, and $|q-q_0|\le\varepsilon/(1-\varepsilon)$ on $C$. Choose $0<\varepsilon<1/4$ so small that this last bound is less than $a-m$ and $b(1+\varepsilon^2/2)<1$. Then $K\subset\{|q|<a\}$. On $A_+$ the numerator equals $d_0$, so $q\ge1$, and the negative counterpart gives $q\le-1$ on $A_-$. Positivity of $d$ also holds on a neighborhood of $[-1,1]$, where the displayed formula defines a smooth $q$.

On $[0,1]$ we have $d'(z)=z/\sqrt{z^2+\varepsilon^2}-2z\le1$. This function is concave, since its second derivative is $-3\varepsilon^2z/(z^2+\varepsilon^2)^{5/2}\le0$, so its minimum is at an endpoint. The endpoint values are $0$ and $1/\sqrt{1+\varepsilon^2}-2\ge-1-\varepsilon^2/2$, the latter inequality following by differentiating $(1+t)^{-1/2}-1+t/2$ for $t\ge0$. Since $d'$ is odd, $|d'|\le1+\varepsilon^2/2$ on $[-1,1]$. Therefore the level equation $F_h(x,y,z)=z+x^2-y^2-hd(z)=0$ has $\partial_zF_h=1-hd'(z)>0$ whenever $|h|\le b$. Each such level is a smooth graph on its projected domain by [F2], with at most one point above each projected point. At $x=y=0$ its equation has exactly one root in $(-1,1)$, because $d(1)=d(-1)=g(1)<1$, so the endpoint values have opposite signs.

For $|z|<1$, put $H_h(z)=(z-hg(z))/(1-z^2)$. Its derivative has numerator $1+z^2-hA(z)$, where $A(z)=(1-z^2)g'(z)+2zg(z)$. For $0\le z\le1$, the definition gives $A\ge0$ and the identity $A=\frac{z}{\sqrt{z^2+\varepsilon^2}}(1+z^2)+2\varepsilon z\bigl(\frac{\varepsilon}{\sqrt{z^2+\varepsilon^2}}-1\bigr)$ gives $A\le1+z^2$. Oddness gives $|A(z)|\le1+z^2$ for negative $z$ as well. Hence $H_h'>0$. Also $H_h(z)\to\pm\infty$ as $z\to\pm1$, since $|hg(1)|<1$. Thus for every angle $\theta$ the equation $H_h(z)=h-\cos(2\theta)$ has a unique smooth root $z_\theta\in(-1,1)$. These are exactly the points of $D_h\cap\partial C$ with projected polar angle $\theta$.

The projected radial domain of $D_h$ contains the origin by step 3.1. On each projected ray its points form a closed subset of $[0,1]$; membership can change only at a sphere-boundary point, because every interior solution persists by [F2]. Step 4.1 gives exactly one sphere-boundary point on that ray, at the positive radius $r_\theta=\sqrt{1-z_\theta^2}$. Consequently that radial domain is exactly $0\le r\le r_\theta$. The boundary radius is smooth and positive, so this is a smooth star-shaped disk, and its graph is a proper smooth disk. For $h_2>h_1$, evaluating $F_{h_2}$ at a zero of $F_{h_1}$ gives $-(h_2-h_1)d<0$, so strict increase in $z$ places the second graph above the first wherever both are defined.

On the equator, the level equation becomes $x^2+y^2=1$ and $x^2-y^2=h$. Its four solutions satisfy $x^2=(1+h)/2$ and $y^2=(1-h)/2$, so all four lie in the open quadrants. Step 4.1 shows that $z_\theta$ has the sign of $h-\cos(2\theta)$: its defining increasing function has $H_h(0)=0$. It follows that the boundary has two positive-$z$ arcs around the $y$ directions and two negative-$z$ arcs around the $x$ directions. The four zeros are simple because $\sin(2\theta)\ne0$ there.

Define $V=(x,y,-2(x^2-y^2)/(1-qd'))$ on a neighborhood of the closed level band; its denominator is positive by step 3.1 and compactness. Differentiating $F_h$ shows $dq(V)=0$, and $V$ is zero exactly when $x=y=0$. On the sphere boundary put $t=\cos(2\theta)$ and $r^2=1-z^2>0$. Then $V(x^2+y^2+z^2)=2r^2(1-hd'-2zt)/(1-hd')$. The boundary equation $t=h-H_h(z)$ gives $1-hd'-2zt=(1+z^2-hA(z))/(1-z^2)>0$ by step 4.1. Thus $V$ points strictly outward there; in particular the level disks meet the sphere transversely.

Steps 1.1–2.1 place $K$ in a middle level band avoiding both link arcs. Steps 3.1–6.1 give the smooth ordered quadrilateral disks, and step 6.2 gives the asserted level-tangent outward radial vector field. All parameter choices used finitely many strict real inequalities and all implicit solutions were unique, so no choice principle has been introduced.

boundaries.evidence: Step 1.1 treats an empty compact set by m=0.
The level h=0 is included in steps 3.1–6.1.
Steps 3.1–6.1 apply to each individual supplied level.

Let $C=\{(x,y,z):x^2+y^2+z^2\le1\}$, with upper overpass $A_+=\{y=0,x^2+z^2=1,z\ge0\}$ and lower underpass $A_-=\{x=0,y^2+z^2=1,z\le0\}$. For every compact $K\subset C\setminus(A_+\cup A_-)$ there are $0<a<b<1$ and $0<\varepsilon<1/4$ such that, on a neighborhood of $C$, the smooth function
$$q(x,y,z)=\frac{z+x^2-y^2}{d(z)},\qquad d(z)=1+\sqrt{z^2+\varepsilon^2}-\varepsilon-z^2$$
has these properties:

1. $K\subset\{|q|<a\}$, $q\ge1$ on $A_+$ and $q\le-1$ on $A_-$.
2. For each $|h|\le b$, $D_h=C\cap q^{-1}(h)$ is a smooth proper disk transverse to $\partial C$. Projection to the $(x,y)$-plane identifies it with a smooth star-shaped disk. Its boundary meets $z=0$ in exactly four points, one in each open quadrant; its intersections with each open hemisphere are two arcs. The disks are disjoint and strictly ordered by height above every common projected point.
3. On $C\cap\{|q|\le b\}$ there is a smooth vector field $V$ tangent to the levels of $q$, with $(V_x,V_y)=(x,y)$, zero exactly on the vertical axis, and pointing strictly outward on $\partial C\cap\{|q|\le b\}$. Consequently radial dilation in these level coordinates is compatible with the boundary of the crossing ball.

This supplies the local foliation and vector field, not an ambient positioning theorem for a surface.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $\mathcal F:M\times S\to N$ be a smooth family of maps and let $Z\subseteq N$
be an embedded submanifold. If $\mathcal F\pitchfork Z$, then the set of
parameters $s\in S$ for which the slice $\mathcal F_s:M\to N$ fails to be
transverse to $Z$ is a null subset of $S$.

Assume countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $A$ be a closed subset of a smooth manifold $M$, and let $U\subseteq M$ be open with $A\subseteq U$. Then there exists a smooth function $f:M\to[0,1]$ such that $f=1$ on an open neighbourhood of $A$ and $\operatorname{supp}(f)\subseteq U$.

derivations.claim: First work with one ball $C$. The compact set $K=S\cap C$ misses its two crossing arcs, so apply [F1] to get $a,b,q,V$. On the closed middle band the coordinates $(x,y,h)=(x,y,q)$ are nonsingular: the explicit foliation proof gives $\partial_z(z+x^2-y^2-hd(z))>0$. The compact band misses $L$, since all of $L\cap C$ consists of the two arcs with $|q|\ge1$. Hence it has a neighborhood contained in $W\setminus L$. Every compact set used below can be supported in that neighborhood, or in the interior of $C$ away from $L$.

Make $S$ transverse to the open vertical axis $J=\{x=y=0,-1<z<1\}$. Its current intersection with this axis is compact and away from the endpoints, because those endpoints belong to $L$ and $S$ misses them. Choose a smooth coordinate cutoff $\eta$, supported inside $\operatorname{int}C\setminus L$ and equal to one near this compact intersection, using [F3]. For small parameters $v=(v_1,v_2)$, the coordinate maps $T_v(x,y,z)=(x+\eta v_1,y+\eta v_2,z)$ are ambient diffeomorphisms, extended by the identity: taking $|v|\sup|D\eta|<1$ makes the perturbation globally injective with invertible derivative, and its compact support makes it onto. Compactness ensures that any intersection $T_v(S)\cap J$ for sufficiently small $v$ occurs where $\eta=1$. There the parameter derivative spans the two normal directions to $J$, so the evaluation family on $S$ is transverse to $J$. Apply [F2] to select an arbitrarily small transverse parameter. The path $T_{tv}$ is an ambient isotopy fixing $L$. Choose the parameter small enough that the new $S\cap C$ remains in $|q|<a$; this follows from the original strict compact margin and the fact that these maps are supported inside $C$. Its intersection with $J$ is now finite, since it is compact and transverse of dimension zero. If the initial intersection was empty, omit this perturbation.

Choose a smooth nonnegative function $\chi(h)$ equal to one for $|h|\le a$ and supported in $|h|<b$. The field $\chi(q)V$ is smooth on $C$, zero off the middle band and disjoint from $L$. The formula for $V$ extends to a neighborhood of the closed band by [F1]. Multiply this extension by a spatial cutoff equal to one near that band and supported in a sufficiently small neighborhood inside $W\setminus L$, and extend by zero to $S^3$. Call the resulting field $X$. It is smooth, compactly supported, and its boundary-normal component on $\partial C$ is nonnegative everywhere and strictly positive wherever $\chi(q)>0$. Consequently no forward integral curve can enter $\operatorname{int}C$ from outside: near a boundary point with positive component the signed exterior coordinate is strictly increasing, and a boundary point with zero component has $X=0$ and its integral curve is stationary by uniqueness. Thus the backward trajectory of any point in $\operatorname{int}C$ stays in $C$ for its whole backward time interval.

Write the finitely many axis intersections as $(0,0,h_i)$ in the level coordinates. Their $h_i$ are distinct and satisfy $|h_i|<a$. Transversality to $J$ expresses the surface near each as $h=H_i(x,y)$, with $H_i(0,0)=h_i$. Choose disjoint small height intervals around the $h_i$, and cylinders in their interiors and inside $\operatorname{int}C\cap\{|q|<a\}$. In each cylinder choose a height cutoff $\chi_i$ equal to one near $h_i$ and a radial cutoff $\psi_i$ equal to one near the axis. Shrink its projected radius until $|H_i-h_i|\sup|\chi_i'|<1/2$ and its graph stays in the region where $\chi_i=1$. Then the maps $(x,y,h)\mapsto(x,y,h-t\psi_i(x,y)\chi_i(h)(H_i(x,y)-h_i))$ for $0\le t\le1$ are smooth diffeomorphisms: their height derivative is positive, and they are the identity near every cylinder boundary. Extend them by the identity and compose over the disjoint cylinders. They fix $L$ and make $S$ exactly the level $h=h_i$ near each axis intersection, while keeping $S\cap C$ in $|q|<a$.

Compactness of the surface after step 3.1 gives $\delta>0$ such that every point of $S\cap C$ with projected radius $r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}\le\delta$ lies on one of the flattened patches $h=h_i$. Indeed these patches contain all points on the axis; the compact remainder after removing smaller open patches has positive distance from the axis. If there are no axis intersections, the same compactness gives $S\cap C\cap\{r\le\delta\}=\varnothing$. Choose a finite $T>0$ with $e^{-T}<\delta$, and let $\Phi_t$ be the flow of $X$ up to time $T$ supplied by [F4].

If $p\in\Phi_T(S)\cap\operatorname{int}C$, its backward trajectory stays in $C$ by step 2.2, so its initial point $p_0\in S\cap C$ has $|q(p_0)|<a$. While in $C$, $q$ is constant along this trajectory, $\chi=1$, and $\dot x=x$, $\dot y=y$. Thus $r(p_0)=e^{-T}r(p)<\delta$. By step 4.1, $p_0$ lies on a flattened patch with level $h_i$, and therefore $q(p)=h_i$. Hence all of the final surface inside the open ball is contained in the finite disjoint union of these levels. Each axis point $(0,0,h_i)$ is stationary and remains on the surface. For each $i$, the intersection of the final surface with the connected interior of $D_{h_i}$ is closed there, and is open there because the surface is smooth of the same dimension and locally contained in that level. It is nonempty at the stationary axis point. It is therefore the whole disk interior. Closedness of the surface includes each disk boundary as well. There are no additional points on $\partial C$: a boundary point where $\chi(q)>0$ immediately enters the ball under the backward flow, so the same argument puts it on a level $h_i$; a boundary point where $\chi(q)=0$ is stationary, and was not on the initial surface because that surface had $|q|<a$. Thus $\Phi_T(S)\cap C=\bigcup_iD_{h_i}$. In the empty case the intersection is empty.

The level disks are transverse to the boundary and have the required quadrilateral boundaries by [F1]; equality on their interiors also identifies their tangent planes with those of the final surface along the boundary, so the surface itself is transverse there. The perturbation, flattening maps and radial flow all have compact support disjoint from $L$, so together they fix a neighborhood of $S\cap L$. Reparametrize their finitely many time intervals by smooth stationary-end functions and concatenate them to obtain one smooth ambient isotopy.

Finally choose pairwise disjoint open coordinate neighborhoods of the finitely many disjoint compact balls inside $W$. Carry out the preceding construction for each ball with support in its own neighborhood, always disjoint from $L$. The constructions do not affect the results in the other balls and their finite composition has all the asserted support and fixed-point properties. No condition on complementary pieces was used or concluded.

boundaries.evidence: Steps 2.1, 4.1 and 5.1 include no axis intersections; step 7.1 allows no crossing balls.
Step 5.1 proves that zero axis intersections give an empty final ball intersection.
Steps 3.1–5.1 include a single flattened patch and one resulting saddle.
